titre: Avogadro never knew the number that bears his name
accroche: The name dates from 1909 and comes from Jean Perrin. Avogadro, who died in 1856, never tried to count molecules.
contenu_vulgarise:
Who was the first to count the 6.022 × 10²³ entities in a mole? The usual answer is Amedeo Avogadro, whose name is on the number. He never tried to count molecules. The name dates from 1909, and it was Jean Perrin who gave it.

## What Avogadro proposed

In 1811, Avogadro put forward that equal volumes of gas, at the same temperature and pressure, contain the same number of molecules, whatever the gas. The idea serves to compare masses: if two gases occupy the same volume for different masses, the ratio of those masses is the ratio of their molecules. Cannizzaro brought it back to the fore in a pamphlet in 1858, then at the Karlsruhe congress in 1860, four years after Avogadro's death, and it became the basis for determinations of molecular masses.

But the hypothesis gives a ratio, not a count. Perrin puts it in 1926: if molecules and atoms exist, their relative weights are known, and their absolute weights would be known at the same time as Avogadro's number.

## A number born of kinetic theory

According to the historian William Jensen, Avogadro had nothing to do with determining this number. The urge to calculate how many molecules a volume of gas contains was born of kinetic theory, in the second half of the 19th century. The result was then given per milliliter of gas, and took the name “Loschmidt number,” after Josef Loschmidt, who proposed a method for estimating it in 1865. Perrin reports that the values obtained this way, scaled to one gram-molecule, ranged from 40 to 120 × 10²², with an uncertainty that easily reached 100%.

## Perrin and his resin grains

The gram-molecule is the mass of gas that occupies the same volume as 32 grams of oxygen. In his first papers of 1908, Perrin speaks simply of the number of particles per “gram-molecule.” In 1909, in a 144-page review, he proposes to christen this universal invariant the “Avogadro constant.”

He measures it on resin grains suspended in water, which he treats as the visible molecules of a gas: their distribution by height, their Brownian agitation, their fluctuations in concentration give 68, 62, 60, 64 and 65 × 10²² depending on the method, or 64 × 10²² as a rough average. Other independent routes land on the same order of magnitude: from 61 to 75 × 10²² with critical opalescence, the blue of the sky, blackbody radiation, the charge of tiny particles or the counting of helium atoms produced by radioactivity. This agreement is Perrin's argument for the reality of molecules, and it largely earned him the 1926 Nobel Prize in Physics.

## The shift

The name took time to catch on. Ramsay cites it as early as 1912, but “Avogadro's number” did not become a standard entry in American college textbooks until the 1930s, and remained rare in high school textbooks before the 1950s.

The number has also changed status. Since May 20, 2019, the International System of Units fixes by definition that a mole contains exactly 6.022 140 76 × 10²³ elementary entities, whereas it was previously defined by the number of atoms in 0.012 kilogram of carbon 12. This number is therefore no longer measured: it is what defines the mole. It remains to be seen what Avogadro's name then designates, a hypothesis about gases or a choice of convention.

repere.texte: The first estimates of the number of molecules in a gram-molecule, by the kinetic theory of gases, ranged from 40 to 120 × 10²², with an uncertainty that easily reached 100%. From his emulsions, Perrin obtains 64 × 10²² as a rough average.
repere.source: Perrin, “Discontinuous structure of matter,” Nobel lecture, December 11, 1926

carte.punch: Avogadro never knew Avogadro's number: the name dates from Perrin, in 1909.
carte.idee: The 1811 hypothesis compares volumes of gas and gives no number. Loschmidt proposes a method for counting molecules in 1865; Perrin measures it on resin grains, finds 64 × 10²² as a rough average, and christens the constant in 1909.

quiz.question: Why could Avogadro's hypothesis, stated in 1811, not give the number of molecules in a mole?
choix: Because its author did not have enough measurements to test it, and it was rejected before being verified
Because it was rejected until 1909, when Perrin proved that molecules exist
Because it held only for ideal gases, which kept it from applying to real gases
Because it compares volumes of gas and gives ratios of masses, without fixing any absolute size or mass
quiz.explication: The hypothesis establishes ratios between molecular masses. To draw a number from it, you need an absolute quantity (the size or mass of a molecule), which only kinetic theory and then Perrin's experiments supplied. It was not being rejected in 1909: Cannizzaro had brought it back to the fore as early as 1858-1860. The flaw is of another order: it provides only ratios, whatever the gas.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who proposes naming the number of molecules in a gram-molecule the “Avogadro constant,” and when?
choix: Loschmidt, in 1865, in his estimate of the size of air molecules
Perrin, in 1909, in a long review of Brownian motion
Cannizzaro, in 1860, at the Karlsruhe congress that reopens the question of atomic masses
The BIPM, in 2019, when it fixes the value of the number to redefine the mole
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Perrin who writes, in 1909 (*Annales de chimie et de physique* [Annals of Chemistry and Physics]), that this invariant may rightly be called the Avogadro constant. Loschmidt gave his name to a number per milliliter, and the BIPM fixed the value much later.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Perrin obtain his estimate of the number from emulsions?
choix: By weighing resin grains one by one, then dividing the total mass by their number
By counting under a microscope the water molecules surrounding each resin grain
By treating resin grains in suspension as visible molecules of a gas, whose distribution by height and agitation he measures
By measuring the falling speed of a single grain in pure water at constant temperature
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Perrin applies the gas laws to emulsions of equal grains: their equilibrium distribution and their Brownian motion give Avogadro's number. The emulsions give the constant directly; no molecule is counted one by one.
